verdict.text:
Track 1 is measurable here, since scope (34) and condition (21) have real support, but the headline 0% flag rate on those slots is most likely a scoring artifact rather than fabrication. In the worst examples (496-Signal, 592-Signal, 107-Mastodon) the LLM output has no scope or condition phrase at all. It starts directly with "<MISSING_ACTOR> <MISSING_MODAL_VERB> ...". The parser appears to label a slot "filled" whenever no MISSING tag is present, so silent omission is counted as invention. Genuine scope filling does occur in a few cases, such as 828-Signal ("For each TextSecure group"), 1504-Signal and 937-Signal, where a phrase was lifted from the title. These cases are a small minority. Until the parser distinguishes "omitted" from "filled", the scope and condition numbers say little about hallucination.

The actor and modalVerb slots show the dominant real behaviour, and it runs in the opposite direction from fabrication. Humans write "the App must" by convention. Zero-shot Opus instead emits placeholders, flagging 28 of 34 implied modal verbs and 18 of 29 implied actors as missing. This produces 26 of the 35 cases in the "LLM incomplete, gold complete" cell, which makes the overall verdict recall of 1.0 and precision of 0.13 meaningless. Without being told the convention, the model is over-cautious rather than inventive. The actor and modalVerb F1 scores rest on one gold-missing case each, so they cannot be interpreted.

Action is the one slot where silent filling is plausibly real. Of the four gold-missing actions, three were filled (83-, 496- and 592-Signal). Even so, the gold itself is shaky there. For 592, one annotator wrote "provide emojis", and 496's title states the feature outright. With a support of 4, this is anecdote, not a rate.

On similarity, the LLM trails the human-human ceiling by about 0.12 on seq_ratio and Jaccard and about 0.06 on cosine. That gap is partly structural. All three humans share the "<MISSING_SCOPE>, <MISSING_CONDITION>, the App must" template, which inflates their agreement with each other. The LLM omits that prefix. Given standard deviations of about 0.2 and 105 non-independent pairs from 35 items, the cosine gap is within noise. The string-level gap is confounded by template differences, not clearly a content difference.

Paska's 11% pass rate largely mirrors the same convention problem. "Not requirement" (18) and "Incomplete requirement" (14) fire because a sentence opening with placeholder tokens has no parseable system response. The 2/30 versus 2/5 pass split by LLM verdict confirms this. Several smell segment IDs (rimay_2, rimay_3 on 245-, 316-, 5529-, 5775- and 937-Signal) show the model emitted multiple sentences for requirements already judged atomic. That deserves inspection, as does the single "Non-atomic" flag on 6457-Signal, which may be a Paska false positive. Paska has not been run on the human gold, so there is no baseline for how often legitimate placeholder-bearing outputs fail.

Overall, this run mostly measures a format and convention mismatch, not the model's tendency to fabricate. Thirty-five atomic requirements are too few to support slot-level claims beyond scope and condition, and the results should not be generalised to non-atomic input.

The most useful next steps, in order, are:
1. Fix the slot parser so an absent slot is not counted as filled.
2. State the Rimay convention in the prompt: always emit all five slots, and default to "the App must" when the actor is implied.
3. Normalise or strip templates before computing similarity.
4. Run Paska on the human gold to get a baseline.

Then rerun zsl before comparing it with fsl or cot.
